Section syllabus grammar rule: Adverbial pronouns y and en. Explanation: The adverbial pronoun 'y' replaces phrases introduced by à, en, dans, sur (places or inanimate objects). The pronoun 'en' replaces phrases introduced by de, partitive constructions, and indefinite quantities.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Comparative formation: plus... que, moins... que, aussi... que. Explanation: Comparisons of adjectives and adverbs are formed using: plus... que (more... than), moins... que (less... than), and aussi... que (as... as). Adjectives agree in gender and number with the subject being compared.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Disjunctive (stress) pronouns: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles. Explanation: Disjunctive (stress) pronouns (moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles) are used after prepositions (avec moi, sans lui), after c’est (c’est moi), in comparisons (plus grand que lui), and for emphatic subject contrast.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Subject agreement with être in compound tenses. Explanation: Verbs conjugated with être in compound tenses agree in gender and number with the grammatical subject: add -e for feminine, -s for masculine plural, and -es for feminine plural.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Idiomatic expressions with faire. Explanation: Faire enters into numerous idiomatic expressions for weather (il fait beau/chaud), sports and physical activities (faire du sport, faire du vélo), and household tasks (faire la cuisine, faire le ménage).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Idiomatic uses of aller. Explanation: Aller is used idiomatically to inquire about health (Comment allez-vous? / Je vais bien), to indicate suitability (Ça te va bien), and as a semi-auxiliary for the futur proche (aller + infinitive).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Imparfait with depuis and venait de. Explanation: The imparfait with 'depuis' indicates an action that had been going on in the past when another event occurred. 'Venait de + infinitif' expresses an immediate past relative to a past time frame ('had just done').

Section syllabus grammar rule: Indefinite relative pronouns: ce qui, ce que, ce dont, ce à quoi. Explanation: Indefinite relative pronouns refer to general ideas without a specific nominal antecedent: ce qui (subject), ce que (direct object), ce dont (object of preposition de), and ce à quoi (object of preposition à).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Subject-verb inversion in questions. Explanation: In formal questions, invert the subject pronoun and verb (e.g., Parles-tu français?). If the 3rd person singular verb ends in a vowel, insert euphonic -t- before il/elle/on (e.g., Parle-t-il?).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Irregular comparatives and superlatives: meilleur and mieux. Explanation: The adjective 'bon' has the irregular comparative 'meilleur' (better) and superlative 'le meilleur' (best). The adverb 'bien' has the irregular comparative 'mieux' (better) and superlative 'le mieux' (best).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Categories of irregular past participles. Explanation: Irregular past participles fall into four principal groups: ending in -u (bu, lu, vu, su, pu, voulu), ending in -is (pris, mis, assis), ending in -it (dit, écrit, fait), and ending in -ert (ouvert, offert, souffert).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Modal verbs: vouloir, pouvoir, devoir. Explanation: The modal verbs vouloir (to want), pouvoir (to be able to), and devoir (to have to / must) are followed directly by an infinitive without a preposition to express volition, ability/permission, and necessity.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Neither... nor negation with ne... ni... ni. Explanation: The negative conjunction ne... ni... ni expresses 'neither... nor'. Omit 'pas' and place 'ne' before the verb, followed by 'ni' before each negated item (e.g., Je ne bois ni thé ni café).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Rules for determining noun gender by noun endings. Explanation: Noun suffixes serve as reliable indicators of gender: endings such as -tion, -sion, -té, -ure, -ence, -ance, -ette tend to be feminine; endings such as -ment, -eau, -isme, -al, -oir tend to be masculine.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Formation of plural nouns and irregular endings. Explanation: Most French nouns form the plural by adding -s. Nouns ending in -s, -x, or -z do not change. Nouns ending in -eau and -eu take -x (châteaux), and most nouns in -al change to -aux (journal -> journaux).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Conjugation patterns of -oir verbs. Explanation: Verbs ending in -oir (devoir, pouvoir, vouloir, savoir, voir, recevoir) are irregular with characteristic stem alterations between singular and plural forms in the present tense.

Section syllabus grammar rule: The partitive articles: du, de la, de l’, des. Explanation: The partitive article expresses an indefinite quantity of an uncountable noun or mass noun: du (masculine singular), de la (feminine singular), de l' (before vowel/mute h), and des (plural). It translates as 'some' or 'any'.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Partitive reduction with negation and expressions of quantity. Explanation: In negative sentences (with ne... pas, ne... plus, etc.) and after expressions of quantity (beaucoup de, un peu de, trop de, assez de), the partitive articles du, de la, des reduce to 'de' (or 'd'' before a vowel).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Possessive adjectives: agreement and euphonic forms. Explanation: Possessive adjectives (mon, ma, mes; ton, ta, tes; son, sa, ses; notre, nos; votre, vos; leur, leurs) agree in gender and number with the noun possessed. Before feminine nouns beginning with a vowel or mute h, use mon, ton, son.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Possessive pronouns: le mien, le tien, le sien, le nôtre, le vôtre, le leur. Explanation: Possessive pronouns replace a possessive adjective plus noun: le mien / la mienne / les miens / les miennes; le tien; le sien; le nôtre; le vôtre; le leur. They agree in gender and number with the replaced noun.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Pronominal verbs in the passé composé. Explanation: All pronominal verbs take être in compound tenses. The past participle agrees in gender and number with the reflexive pronoun only when the reflexive pronoun is a direct object, not an indirect object.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Relative pronouns où and lequel. Explanation: The relative pronoun 'où' denotes place ('where') and time ('when'). The compound relative pronoun 'lequel' (laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles) is used with prepositions other than de (e.g., sans lequel, pour laquelle).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Hypothetical clauses with plus-que-parfait and past conditional. Explanation: To express hypothetical situations contrary to past fact (regrets and counterfactuals), use Si + plus-que-parfait in the dependent clause and conditionnel passé in the main clause (e.g., Si j’avais su, je serais venu).

Section syllabus grammar rule: Formation and usage of the past subjunctive. Explanation: The past subjunctive (subjonctif passé) is formed using the present subjunctive of avoir or être plus the past participle (e.g., que j’aie fini, que tu sois parti). It expresses a completed action prior to the main clause verb.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Subjunctive triggers: doubt, uncertainty, and denial. Explanation: Verbs expressing doubt, uncertainty, or denial (douter que, ne pas croire que, ne pas penser que, nier que) require the subjunctive mood in the subordinate clause because the reality of the action is unconfirmed.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Subjunctive triggers: emotion and feeling. Explanation: Verbs and impersonal expressions of emotion (être heureux que, regretter que, avoir peur que, être triste que) require the subjunctive in the dependent clause when the subject of the main clause differs from that of the dependent clause.

Section syllabus grammar rule: Conjugation of compounds of venir. Explanation: Compounds of venir (devenir, revenir, convenir, parvenir, se souvenir) conjugate identically to venir in all tenses. Devenir, revenir, and parvenir take être in compound tenses.
